title: Nested Conditions & Multiple Branches 🌲
description: Handle complex logic with nested if and elif chains.

slides.title: Nested if: Inside a Branch 🪆
slides.content:
# Nesting Conditions

You can put an `if` statement inside another `if` (or `else`) block. This lets you test additional conditions only when the outer one is True.

```python
age = 20
has_ticket = True
if age >= 18:
    if has_ticket:
        print("Welcome to the concert!")
    else:
        print("You need a ticket.")
else:
    print("Sorry, this event is 18+.")
```

Indentation clearly shows which block belongs to which `if`.

quizData.question: In the nested example, what prints if age=16 and has_ticket=True?
quizData.explanation: The outer condition `age >= 18` is False, so it jumps to the outer `else` and prints the age restriction message.

slides.title: When to Nest vs. Logical Operators 🔗
slides.content:
## Simplifying with `and` / `or`

Nested `if` can often be replaced by combining conditions with `and`:

```python
# Nested way
if age >= 18:
    if has_ticket:
        print("Entry granted")

# Cleaner way
if age >= 18 and has_ticket:
    print("Entry granted")
```

This reduces indentation levels and makes code more readable. Use nesting only when the inner condition depends on a *unique computation* done inside the outer block.

slides.title: Nested vs Logical Operator
slides.content: Both do the same thing – which do you prefer?

slides.title: Building a Decision Tree 🎄

quizData.question: What if we swapped the first two conditions? `if temperature > 30: print('Hot'); elif temperature > 40: print('Extreme')`? For temp=42, it prints:
quizData.explanation: `42 > 30` is True, so 'Hot' prints and the rest are skipped. The `> 40` condition is never checked, even though it’s also true.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Avoid Deep Nesting

As a rule of thumb, don’t go deeper than 2‑3 levels of indentation. If you find yourself nesting deeper, refactor using functions or logical operators. Deep nesting is hard to read and debug.

slides.title: Putting It Together: User Age Validator 🧪
slides.content:
## Practical Example

Write a snippet that asks for an age (we’ll simulate with a variable) and prints:
- "Child" if under 13
- "Teen" if 13‑17
- "Adult" if 18‑64
- "Senior" if 65+

```python
age = 25
if age < 13:
    print("Child")
elif age < 18:
    print("Teen")
elif age < 65:
    print("Adult")
else:
    print("Senior")
```
Notice we didn’t need a lower bound for each because `elif` only runs if all previous conditions were False.
